title: Which genes can a pathology foundation model see? Cellularity confounding and transcriptome-wide predictability from H&E

authors.name: Author Placeholder
authors.affiliation: Department of Biomedical Engineering / Computer Science

abstract: Predicting spatial transcriptomic profiles directly from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) histology images is widely pursued to augment morphological pathology with molecular measurements. However, prevailing benchmarks evaluate models on un-normalised count targets (log(1+count)) and restricted gene panels, potentially obscuring non-transcriptional confounds. Here, we present a systematic predictability atlas across ~5,000 genes measured by Xenium Prime 5K on 9 human tissue samples spanning six organ sites (lung, ovary, cervix, skin, prostate, lymph node) and 8 leave-one-group-out folds. On raw counts, state-of-the-art pathology foundation models (Virchow2, UNI2-h, CONCH v1.5) achieve gene-averaged Pearson correlations up to r=0.519, closely matched by a scalar nuclear count alone (r=0.445) and broad lineage composition (r=0.490). Crucially, upon standard library-size normalisation (lognorm), predictive performance collapses to r=0.193 (Virchow2) and r=0.148 (UNI2-h), failing to exceed trivial cell counts (r=0.214) or data-driven unsupervised single-cell cluster composition (r=0.207, 0.000 unassigned cells). Spot cellularity accounts for R^2=0.953 of cross-gene variance on raw counts, whereas residual predictability on normalised targets is driven primarily by cell-type specificity and cross-encoder agreement (R^2=0.610). Our findings indicate that apparent high predictability from histology images largely reflects local cellularity estimation rather than de novo prediction of intrinsic transcriptional regulation.
